title: The physician sent to sinners
source_text: Εἶτα συκοφαντῶν τὰ προτροπῆς ἕνεκα εἰρημένα καὶ γεγραμμένα τῆς πρὸς τοὺς κακῶς βεβιωκότας καὶ καλοῦντα αὐτοὺς ἐπὶ μετάνοιαν καὶ διόρθωσιν τῆς ψυχῆς αὐτῶν, φησὶν ἡμᾶς λέγειν τοῖς ἁμαρτωλοῖς πεπέμφθαι τὸν θεόν, ὅμοιον δὲ καὶ τοῦτο ποιεῖ, ὡς εἰ ἐνεκάλει τισὶ λέγουσι διὰ τοὺς κακῶς διάγοντας ἐν τῇ πόλει πεπέμφθαι ὑπὸ φιλανθρωποτάτου βασιλέως τὸν ἰατρόν, ἐπέμφθη οὖν θεὸς λόγος καθὸ μὲν ἰατρὸς τοῖς ἁμαρτωλοῖς, καθὸ δὲ διδάσκαλος θείων μυστηρίων τοῖς ἤδη καθαροῖς καὶ μηκέτι ἁμαρτάνουσιν. ὁ δὲ Κέλσος ταῦτα μὴ δυνηθεὶς διακρῖναι (οὐ γὰρ ἠβουλήθη φιλομαθῆσαι) φησί· τί δὲ τοῖς ἀναμαρτήτοις οὐκ ἐπέμφθη; τί κακόν ἐστι τὸ μὴ ἡμαρτηκέναι; καὶ πρὸς τοῦτό φαμεν ὅτι, εἰ μὲν ἀναμαρτήτους λέγει τοὺς μηκέτι ἁμαρτάνοντας, ἐπέμφθη καὶ τούτοις ὁ σωτὴρ ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦς, ἀλλ᾿ οὐχ ὡς ἰατρός· εἰ δ᾿ ἀναμαρτήτοις τοῖς μηδεπώποτε ἡμαρτηκόσιν (οὐ γὰρ διεστείλατο ἐν τῇ ἑαυτοῦ λέξει), ἐροῦμεν ὅτι ἀδύνατον εἶναι οὕτως ἄνθρωπον ἀναμάρτητον, τοῦτο δέ φαμεν ὑπεξαιρουμένου τοῦ κατὰ τὸν Ἰησοῦν νοουμένου ἀνθρώπου, „ὃς ἁμαρτίαν οὐκ ἐποίησε.“ κακούργως δή φησιν ὁ Κέλσος περὶ ἡμῶν ὡς δὴ φασκόντων ὅτι τὸν μὲν ἄδικον, ἐὰν αὑτὸν ὑπὸ μοχθηρίας ταπεινώσῃ, δέξεται ὁ θεὸς, τὸν δὲ δίκαιον, ἐὰν μετ᾿ ἀρετῆς ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς ἄνω πρὸς αὐτὸν βλέπῃ, τοῦτον οὐ δέξεται, ἀδύνατον (γάρ) φαμεν εἶναι ἄνθρωπον μετ᾿ ἀρετῆς ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς πρὸς τὸν θεὸν ἄνω βλέπειν· κακίαν γὰρ ὑφίστασθαι ἀναγκαῖον πρῶτον ἐν ἀνθρώποις, καθὸ καὶ ὁ Παῦλος λέγει· „ἐλθούσης δὲ τῆς ἐντολῆς ἡ ἁμαρτία ἀνέζησεν, ἐγὼ δὲ ἀπέθανον“· ἀλλὰ καὶ οὐ διδάσκομεν περὶ τοῦ ἀδίκου ὅτι αὔταρκες αὐτῷ τὸ διὰ τὴν μοχθηρίαν ἑαυτὸν ταπεινοῦν πρὸς τὸ δεχθῆναι ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ, ἀλλ᾿ ἐὰν μὲν ἐπὶ τοῖς προτέροις ἑαυτοῦ καταγνοὺς πορεύηται „ταπεινὸς“ ἐπ᾿ ἐκείνοις καὶ „κεκοσμημένος“ ἐπὶ τοῖς δευτέροις, τοῦτον παραδέξεται ὁ θεός.
pass_a_gloss: Then slandering (συκοφαντέω) the things said and written for the sake of exhortation (προτροπή) to those who have lived badly, calling them to repentance (μετάνοια) and correction (διόρθωσις) of their soul, he says we say that God has been sent (πέμπω, pf. pass.) to sinners (ἁμαρτωλός). He does something like this, as if he accused (ἐγκαλέω) some who say that because of those faring badly (κακῶς διάγω) in the city the physician (ἰατρός) had been sent by a most humane (φιλανθρωπότατος) king. So God the Word (θεὸς λόγος) was sent: insofar as physician, to sinners; insofar as teacher (διδάσκαλος) of divine mysteries (μυστήριον), to those already pure (καθαρός) and no longer sinning. Celsus, unable to distinguish (διακρίνω) these (for he did not wish to love learning, φιλομαθέω), says: 'Why was he not sent to the sinless (ἀναμάρτητος)? What evil is it not to have sinned?' We say: if he calls sinless those no longer sinning, our Saviour (σωτήρ) Jesus was sent to these too, but not as physician; if the sinless are those who never at any time sinned (for he did not distinguish, διαστέλλομαι, in his own wording, λέξις), we shall say it is impossible for a human being to be sinless thus; this we say excepting (ὑπεξαιρέω) the man understood (νοέω) in the case of Jesus, 'who did no sin'. Celsus says maliciously (κακούργως) of us, as though we asserted that the unjust (ἄδικος), if he humbles (ταπεινόω) himself by reason of wickedness (μοχθηρία), God will receive (δέχομαι); but the just (δίκαιος), if with virtue (ἀρετή) from the beginning he looks up (ἄνω βλέπω) to him, him he will not receive. (For) we say it is impossible for a human being with virtue from the beginning to look up to God; for evil (κακία) must necessarily (ἀναγκαῖον) first subsist (ὑφίστημι) in human beings, as Paul says: 'the commandment (ἐντολή) having come, sin revived (ἀναζάω), and I died.' Moreover we do not teach of the unjust that humbling himself because of wickedness is sufficient (αὔταρκες) for being received by God; but if, having condemned (καταγιγνώσκω) himself for his former things, he walks humble (ταπεινός) over those and ordered (κεκοσμημένος, κοσμέω) in the later ones, him God will accept (παραδέχομαι).

lemmas.lemma: for he did not wish to love learning, φιλομαθέω
for he did not distinguish, διαστέλλομαι, in his own wording, λέξις

pass_b_english: Next he misrepresents what has been said and written to exhort those who have lived badly, calling them to repentance (Luke 5:32) and to the reform of their souls, and he says that we claim God was sent to sinners. In this too he acts like someone who would find fault with people for saying that a most humane king had sent the physician because of those in the city who were in a bad way. So God the Word was sent: as physician to sinners (Matthew 9:12), and as teacher of divine mysteries to those who are already pure and no longer sin.

Celsus could not tell these apart, for he did not care to learn, and he says: "Why was he not sent to those without sin? What evil is it not to have sinned?" To this we say that if by "those without sin" he means those who no longer sin, then our Saviour Jesus was sent to them too, though not as a physician. But if he means those who have never sinned at all (for he made no distinction in his wording), we shall say that no human being can be without sin in that sense. We say this while making an exception of the man understood in Jesus, "who committed no sin" (1 Peter 2:22).

Celsus speaks maliciously about us, as though we claimed that "God will receive the unjust man if he humbles himself because of his wickedness, but will not receive the just man if he looks up to him with virtue from the beginning." We say that it is impossible for a human being to look up to God with virtue from the beginning. For evil must first exist in human beings, as Paul too says: "When the commandment came, sin came to life again, and I died" (Romans 7:9-10). Nor do we teach about the unjust man that it is enough for him to humble himself because of his wickedness in order to be received by God. Rather, if he condemns himself for his former deeds and walks "humble" over them, and "well ordered" in his later conduct (Plato, Laws 716a), God will accept him.

choices.choice: Celsus's charge 'God was sent to sinners' is reported indirectly (φησὶν ἡμᾶς λέγειν) and is left without quotation marks; his direct questions and the clause introduced by ὡς δὴ φασκόντων are quoted. The clause 'calling them to repentance' echoes Luke 5:32 (καλέσαι ... ἁμαρτωλοὺς εἰς μετάνοιαν), and 'physician to sinners' takes up Matthew 9:12, which Origen quoted in 3.61; both are cited as allusions (Mark 2:17 is parallel to Matthew 9:12). 'Who committed no sin' is 1 Peter 2:22, itself from Isaiah 53:9 LXX (ἀνομίαν οὐκ ἐποίησεν); Origen's wording matches Peter. Romans 7:9 ends at ἀνέζησεν and 7:10 begins ἐγὼ δὲ ἀπέθανον, so both verses are cited. κακῶς διάγοντας in the king simile can mean 'living badly' or 'faring badly / sick'; rendered 'in a bad way' to keep both. 'The man understood in Jesus' keeps Origen's distinction between the Word and the human being Jesus (κατὰ τὸν Ἰησοῦν νοουμένου ἀνθρώπου). The bracketed (γάρ) before ἀδύνατον is an editorial supplement; it is translated by the causal sense of the sentence without an explicit 'for'. 'Humble' and 'well ordered' (ταπεινὸς ... κεκοσμημένος) are Plato's words from Laws 716a, which Origen names in 3.63.
'In this he acts' -> 'In this too he acts' (καὶ τοῦτο)
'We say this making an exception' -> 'We say this while making an exception' (smoother English)
κεκοσμημένος: 'orderly' -> 'well ordered' (closer to the participle; kept consistent with 3.63)
Checked: Luke 5:32, Matthew 9:12, 1 Peter 2:22, Romans 7:9-10 (7:10 opens with ἐγὼ δὲ ἀπέθανον), Plato Laws 716a; speaker framing for Celsus's questions and charge correct
